newsitem.title: FRANCE: OPINION - What kind of EMU? - By Patrick Artus.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - What kind of EMU? - By Patrick Artus.

text.p: By Patrick Artus, Head of Economic Research, Caisses des Depots et Consignations
Several months ago the whole process of European monetary union seemed to be clearly mapped out in everbody's mind.
A relatively small number would tie their currencies -- the "core" countries: Germany, France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria -- and the remainder would wait outside until later.
Even those in the front line to join would have a very hard time meeting the criteria laid down in the Maastricht treaty, above all on public deficits.

But, the theory went, this would not be so tough because the process of choosing the qualifiers, a choice to be made in 1998, would be a political one, which allowed a degree of flexibility in interpreting those criteria.
THE NEW VERSION OF EVENTS:

However, things have changed in the last few months and this view of how it would all work out has changed dramatically, on two levels. It now looks like the criteria will be interpreted to the letter.

Those who want in will have to show a deficit in 1997 which is actually less than three percent of gross domestic product; and in return, governments (France, Spain...) have learned how to exploit the differences between deficit accounting for the purposes of Maastricht and traditional deficit accounting at national level.
This allows them to call on one-off receipts to reduce a "photo-shot" deficit.
This change of track started with France and many others followed suit. Now, France, Italy, Spain, Belgium, Portugal and Sweden have all announced deficits of three percent of GDP for 1997.

And so, the probability (whether real or as it is perceived by the markets) of countries other than the "core" group being ready to join at the start in 1999 has increased, with extremely restrictive budget policies to rein in public deficits to three percent (or a level where the one-off receipts bridge the gap).

This twist in events has triggered a strong convergence of long-term interest rates (Italian, Spanish and Swedish...) with those of Germany and the depreciation of the mark versus all the other currencies.

Another thing that seems clear; some of the countries truly set on taking part from the start in 1999 will not have to place this decision in the context of the gap between their economic structure and those of Germany (level of development, wealth per person, structure of employment or of production).
These changes in the perception of the unification process raise a number of questions;
First of all, why the sudden choice of going for a deficit of effectively less than three percent?

Probably because they realised that Germany -- whether the government, public opinion, the Bundesbank or the Bundestag -- would not tolerate flexible interpretation of deficit criteria and that they had to get under three percent in 1997 to avoid being rejected or to avoid giving Germany a pretext to delay the whole thing.
WILL THERE BE MANY COUNTRIES IN MONETARY UNION IN 1999?
This then begs the question of whether all countries will in fact reduce their public deficits in time.
The most critical case is undoubtedly Italy, the only large country whose intention of making the rendezvous is clear but whose situation in terms of the public deficit is difficult.

The Italian public deficit will probably still be too high in 1997, with a high starting point of six percent in 1996 and accelerating pace in wage rises (more than five percent in the last 12 months) which risk stopping the disinflation process above the three percent inflation mark.

And we already know that the Bank of Italy will only allow substantial cuts in short-term rates if inflation comes below this level, which is vital to reduce interest payments on the country's debt and deficit.

Also, Italian economic growth is weak -- with less than one percent in 1996 and 1.5 percent without doubt in 1997 -- and the introduction of an additional "Europe-tax" will add a further brake on growth and fiscal receipts.
The likelihood of Italy joining in monetary union in 1999 is therefore fairly slim, a view which is perhaps not the market consensus at the moment.
WIDESPREAD OR LIMITED MONETARY UNION: WHAT WILL THEY MEAN?
So, what would be the consequences of the two possibilities, a generalised move to monetary union including the countries of southern Europe or a more limited move, notably excluding Italy?

The first scenario involving a large number of countries (a hypothesis likely to irk some of the "core" countries) would produce a single currency zone with a public debt, structural inflation and middling credibility which would be less favourable than those of Germany or France. (Italy's public debt is 120 percent of GDP and inflation in Italy or Spain is still near 3.5 percent.)
This could have contradictory effects:

- Europe would get a poorer "quality" rating in the markets, which would at least initially result in depreciation vis-a-vis other currencies, such as the dollar. On that note, we have seen a slide in the mark recently which is, perhaps, the result of an upward revision of the number of countries expected to tie their currencies in 1999.

- On the other hand, the European Central Bank would end up trying to bolster its credibility at the outset and fighting a level of structural inflation which is still too high, which would result in a fairly restrictive monetary policy.
This, in contrast, is a factor which would favour a strong euro and dampen activity.

In the alternative scenario, especially if a small number of countries (Italy) are left out, the greatest risk is the risk of a crisis triggered by speculative attacks on the currencies left outside (the lira). This risk is all the more threatening to the extent that those left outside would seek to link their currency to the euro in a framework (ERM II) of narrow fluctuation bands.

We already know through theory and past experience that there would be speculative attacks aimed at "breaking" those bands, and hence a risk of volatility and abnormal depreciation of the currencies in question.
Thus both scenarios carry risks: a futilely restrictive monetary policy on the one hand and on the other a speculative crisis and the distortion of currency parities.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters)
